extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society, natural philosophers, astronomers, and mariners (practical observers)
extracted.subtask_short: observational tide and eclipse data collection
extracted.subtask_description: Practical directions and evaluative standards for collecting and reporting observational data about tides and eclipses to test physical hypotheses. Includes what to record, where/how to observe, and what patterns in observations would confirm or refute proposed theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a tide diary (height and time)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good diary of the height and time both of high-water and low-water, for a year or two together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record both the time and perpendicular height of high and low waters regularly over extended periods (a year or two). Prefer observations at several places (Chatham, Greenwich, but preferably some place in the open sea, Land's End, west parts of Ireland, St. Helen's, the Bermudas, etc.) because measurements from open sea or distant stations will better resolve hypotheses than verbal discourse alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record spring tide times and perpendicular heights
rubrics_metrics.description: Make particular observations of all the spring tides (new moon and full moon) noting the hour and the perpendicular height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers (intelligent persons near the sea or upon the sea-shore, watermen, or other residents by the water side) should note hour and perpendicular height for each new- and full-moon spring tide (and also observe low waters). Use simple marks (e.g., on a standing post in the water) to record low-water levels. Collect observations over relevant months (example given: between now and the end of November) to compare seasonal differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate open-sea vs channel observations when analyzing tide timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether observed offsets in the timing of spring tides (e.g., occurring two or three days after new/full moon) are phenomena of the open sea or of narrower channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the timing offset occurs only in channels, seek explanation in local geometry (in-draughts, bays, channels). If it occurs in the open sea as well, seek an explanation rooted in the general hypothesis. Do not conflate effects from channels with open-sea behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for local geographic and meteorological factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular varieties of tides in several parts of the world depend on channels, bays, promontories, gulfs, shallows, currents, trade-winds, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining local tidal behavior, include consideration of channel/bay geometry, vast in-draughts, currents, trade-winds and similar accidents; general hypotheses may be true yet insufficient to predict local peculiarities without detailed local data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify tidal amplitude progression across lunar cycle (sine-proportion hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate in what proportion the increases and decreases, risings and fallings of the tide occur relative to one another; it is supposed they may proceed in the proportion of sines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure successive increases from quarter to spring tide and decreases from spring tide back to quarter, under calm conditions (no wind or other accident). Compare the sequence of increments to a sine-like progression to test the supposition that rises and falls follow sine proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure tidal current velocity profile during flood and ebb
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe that the tidal current's speed sometimes increases from the beginning of the flood to the middle and then decreases toward high water; record velocity versus time to quantify this profile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In equal spaces of time during flood or ebb, measure the increase and decrease of velocity (and corresponding degrees of rising/falling) to test whether these follow the proportion of sines. Use repeated timed measurements along the main sea-shore and note variations caused by local features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use celestial (planetary) positional observations to test the tidal hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Celestial observations (e.g., positional changes of Mars) can give the clearest evidence for the hypothesis about earth/moon motions affecting tides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare observed planetary positions at various lunar phases (first quarter, full, last quarter) with predicted positions under the hypothesis: e.g., if Mars is observed somewhat too backward before full moon and too forward after full moon (with the largest discrepancy at quadratures), that pattern would strongly confirm the hypothesis. If no discernible parallax or positional shift is detected, it constrains the semidiameter of the earth's epicycle to be very small rather than disproving the hypothesis outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report precise, calibrated eclipse observations (times, duration, obscuration)
rubrics_metrics.description: When observing an eclipse, record precise begin/middle/end times, duration, greatest obscurity in digits, apparent diameters, and any unusual features (e.g., limb visibility, atmospheric effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use telescopic projection techniques (e.g., cast the sun's image through a telescope onto extended paper divided into concentric circles and digits) to measure obscuration in 'digits'. Report altitudes, parts of the sun's diameter remaining light/dark, and any perceived atmospheres or libration motions. Provide times to the minute/second where possible and note discrepancies with astronomical tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer confirming new hypotheses by checking prior literature and existing refutations
rubrics_metrics.description: Before undertaking lengthy refutations or repetitions, verify whether the points have already been answered and avoid re-stating refuted arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mathematical or philosophical claims for novelty and prior confutations; if the material 'contains but a repetition of what he had before told us more than once, and which hath been answered long ago', a full confutation may be unnecessary. Also check arguments for internal consistency with established propositions (e.g., Euclid's propositions) and with prior demonstrated results.
